questions.q: Which problem is a "binary search on the answer"?
questions.explain: "The smallest value such that something is possible", with a check you can run for one candidate, is the signal. The others are frequency, sliding-window and two-pointer problems.
options: Count how many times each parcel weight appears
Find the smallest truck capacity that ships every parcel, in order, within 5 days
Find the best 7 consecutive days of revenue
Remove duplicate order ids from a sorted list

questions.q: What property must the check have for binary search on the answer to work?
questions.explain: Binary search needs one test at the middle to tell which side the switch is on. A sorted array is just one source of that property; a monotonic check over numbers is another.
options: It must be fast
It must be monotonic: over the ordered candidates its answers go false, …, false, true, …, true and switch only once
It must return a number
The input array must be sorted

questions.q: Why is "capacity c ships everything within 5 days" monotonic in c?
questions.explain: If c works, c + 1 works too. So the answers over capacities are no, …, no, yes, …, yes, and the first yes is the minimum capacity.
options: Because parcels are sorted by weight
A bigger truck can carry at least what a smaller one carried each day, so it never needs more days
Because the number of parcels is fixed
It is not monotonic

questions.q: What are safe search bounds for the minimum truck capacity?
questions.explain: The lower bound must not exclude the answer, and the upper bound must certainly work. Tighter bounds save a few checks; wrong bounds give wrong answers.
options: From 0 to the number of parcels
From the heaviest parcel (nothing smaller can carry it) to the total weight (ships everything in one day)
From the lightest parcel to the heaviest parcel
From 1 to 1,000,000, always

questions.q: The naive search tries capacities 45, 46, 47, … and each check fails. What does it waste?
questions.explain: Monotonicity means one check rules out a whole side. Testing the middle rules out half of all remaining candidates at once.
options: Nothing; each capacity must be checked
Each failure proves that every smaller capacity also fails, and each success that every bigger one works; stepping by 1 ignores that
Memory
It checks capacities twice

questions.q: The candidate capacities run from 1 to 1,000,000. About how many checks does binary search need?
questions.explain: Each check halves the range: ⌈log₂ 1,000,000⌉ = 20. The range can be enormous; the cost is dominated by what one check costs.
options: About 20
About 500,000

questions.q: One check simulates loading all n parcels. What is the total cost of binary search on capacities between max and total?
questions.explain: Checks × cost per check: about log₂ of the range, each O(n). The naive search is O(n × range), which grows like n² when the range grows with n.
options: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n · log(total − max))
O(n²)

questions.q: What invariant does firstTrue(lo, hi, test) keep?
questions.explain: When lo meets hi, the invariant pins the switch point exactly: everything before is false, everything from there on is true.
options: lo and hi are always true
Every number below lo is false, and every number from hi on is true (or past the end)
The range doubles each step
mid is always false

questions.q: In firstTrue, a true middle sets hi = mid, not hi = mid - 1. Why?
questions.explain: hi = mid goes with while (lo < hi) and an exclusive hi. The loop still ends, because mid < hi always, so the range shrinks every step.
options: To make the loop faster
mid itself might be the first true, so it must stay a candidate; with an exclusive hi, hi = mid keeps it as the boundary
Because mid - 1 could be negative
It is a bug; it should be mid - 1

questions.q: firstTrue(lo, hi, test) is called and no candidate passes. What does it return, and what should the caller do?
questions.explain: For lower bound, returning the array length ("past the end") is meaningful. For a capacity search, returning an untested capacity would be a silent bug if the bounds were wrong.
options: It throws an error automatically
It returns -1
It returns hi, a value that was never tested; the caller must choose an hi that surely works, or check the result
It loops forever

questions.q: How is the lower bound of a sorted array a special case of firstTrue?
questions.explain: Upper bound is the first true of "items[i] > target". Count of a value = upper − lower. One search function answers all of these.
options: It is not; lower bound needs its own algorithm
Over positions 0 to items.length, the test "items[i] >= target" is false then true, and lower bound is its first true
Lower bound is the last false of "items[i] === target"
Lower bound uses firstTrue on the values instead of positions

questions.q: When is bisecting commits to find the first failing build valid?
questions.explain: A flaky test or a bug that was fixed and reintroduced gives several switch points. Bisect then returns one of them, not necessarily the one you care about.
options: Always
When the history is monotonic: every commit after the breaking one also fails, and the test is deterministic
Only when there are fewer than 1,000 commits
Only when commits are sorted by author

questions.q: About how many test runs does bisecting 1,000 commits need?
questions.explain: ⌈log₂ 1,000⌉ = 10. At 8 minutes per run that is about 80 minutes, instead of days when stepping through commits one by one.
options: About 10

questions.q: Why does binary search on the answer pay off most when each check is expensive (a build, a load test)?
questions.explain: With a check that costs microseconds, even a linear scan might be acceptable. With a check that costs 8 minutes, the log is the difference between an hour and a week.
options: Because expensive checks are always monotonic
The total cost is the number of checks times the cost of one; cutting checks from thousands to about ten saves the most when each one takes minutes
Because cheap checks cannot be binary searched
It pays off the same in every case

questions.q: In a rotated sorted array, items[lo] <= items[mid]. What do you know?
questions.explain: There is only one drop, so at least one half is sorted. If the left end is not bigger than the middle, the drop is not in the left half. Then a range check tells you whether the target can be there.
options: The whole array is sorted
The left half, lo to mid, has no drop and is in normal sorted order
The target is in the left half
The rotation point is at mid

questions.q: Why does plain binary search fail on a rotated array such as [40, 50, 60, 10, 20, 30]?
questions.explain: For target 20 the middle is 60; plain search goes left, where only 40 and 50 are. The rotated search first asks which half is sorted.
options: Because it has an even length
"Bigger than the middle means go right" is false across the drop: values bigger than the middle can sit to its left
Because the values are multiples of 10
It does not fail

questions.q: Why can duplicates make rotated-array search O(n)?
questions.explain: In [5, 5, 5, 1, 5] both halves look alike from their ends. Solutions fall back to lo++, which in the worst case visits every element.
options: Duplicates make the array unsorted
When items[lo], items[mid] and items[hi] are equal, nothing tells you which half is sorted, so you can only shrink by one element
Because Map lookups become slow
They cannot; it stays O(log n)

questions.q: Why does the lesson search repayments in whole kobo rather than in naira with decimals?
questions.explain: Search in the smallest unit (kobo, grams, seconds). If you must search real numbers, run a fixed number of halvings instead of waiting for lo to meet hi.
options: Because JavaScript has no decimals
On integers lo < hi ends after a predictable number of halvings and money stays exact; on decimals the range may never become empty
Because kobo searches need more checks
Because binary search only works on arrays

questions.q: What is the benefit of keeping the check (daysNeeded(weights, c) <= maxDays) separate from the search (firstTrue)?
questions.explain: All domain knowledge lives in the check, which you can test on its own. A bug in the check becomes a bug in the answer, so test both.
options: It makes the search faster
The search knows nothing about trucks, so the same tested firstTrue serves capacities, speeds, repayments and commits; only the check changes
It uses less memory
It avoids the need for bounds

questions.q: You need the largest loan whose monthly payment fits a customer's budget. How do you use firstTrue?
questions.explain: "Last true" of a true-then-false test is "first true of its negation, minus one". The same trick finds the largest integer whose square is at most 50.
options: You cannot; firstTrue only finds minimums
Search for the first loan that does not fit (the test is monotonic: once a loan is too big, bigger ones are too) and subtract one
Search for the first loan that fits
Reverse the array first

questions.q: During git bisect run, one test run fails because of a network timeout, not the bug. What happens?
questions.explain: Binary search never looks back at a discarded half. Make the check deterministic (or have the script report "skip", exit code 125, when it cannot decide).
options: Git retries automatically
Bisect trusts the wrong answer, discards the half that contains the real culprit, and confidently names the wrong commit
Bisect ignores that commit
Nothing, because only the last run matters

questions.q: daysNeeded starts a new day when load + w > capacity. What goes wrong with >=?
questions.explain: The search is only as correct as the check. An edge bug in the check silently shifts the answer; test the check on "exactly full" cases.
options: Nothing
A parcel that exactly fills the truck is pushed to the next day, so the check reports too many days and the search returns a capacity that is too large
The search loops forever
It only matters for the first parcel

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first 5 is at position 1 (lower bound); the first value greater than 5 is 8 at position 4 (upper bound); nothing is at least 20, so the result is hi, 6: "past the end". There are 4 − 1 = 3 fives.

questions.q: Which middles does the search test? What does this print?
questions.explain: 8 is false (lo = 9), 12 is true (hi = 12), 10 is false (lo = 11), 11 is true (hi = 11). Now lo = hi = 11: the first true.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: When nothing passes, lo climbs to hi (10), a value outside the candidates 1 to 9. When everything passes, the first candidate, 1, is the answer.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: At 50 kg: day 1 takes 10 + 20 (30 more would make 60), day 2 takes 30, day 3 takes 40. At 60 kg: 10 + 20 + 30, then 40. At 100 kg everything fits in one day.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Two days need 60 kg (10 + 20 + 30, then 40); at 59 kg it takes three. Three days are possible at the smallest candidate, 40 kg (10 + 20, 30, 40).

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A range of 1,000 candidates needs ⌈log₂ 1000⌉ = 10 halvings. Walking up from 0 would have needed 638 checks.

questions.q: Two versions of the check, one with > and one with >=. What does this print?
questions.explain: With >, two 25 kg parcels exactly fill a 50 kg truck: 2 days. With >=, every second parcel is pushed to a new day, so each day carries one parcel: 4 days. A search built on the wrong check would rent a truck twice as big as needed.

questions.q: What does this print? Each result is [position, steps].
questions.explain: For 20: the middle is 60 (position 2); the left half 40..60 is sorted and does not contain 20, so go right; the next middle is position 4, which is 20. For 60 the first middle is the answer. For 35 the search narrows three times and finds nothing.

questions.q: Plain binary search on a rotated array. What does this print?
questions.explain: 50 is found by luck (the middle, 60, sends the search left, where 50 is). 20 is also smaller than 60, so the search goes left too, but 20 is on the right, past the drop. Silent wrong answers are the danger of searching data that does not meet the precondition.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Values before the rotation point (40, 50, 60) are bigger than the last element, 30; values from it on (10, 20, 30) are not. "At most the last element" switches from false to true at position 3: the oldest entry.

questions.q: The test below is not monotonic. What does firstTrue return?
questions.explain: The first middle, 4, is true, so the search looks left; 2 is false, so it looks right; 3 is false, so it settles on 4. The true at position 1 is never seen. Binary search returns a switch point with full confidence; only monotonicity makes it the first true.

questions.q: Write firstTrue(lo, hi, test): the smallest number in lo to hi - 1 for which test is true (or hi if none), using binary search. Print the three results.
questions.explain: 7 × 7 = 49 is below 50, so 8 is the first number whose square is at least 50. Nothing below 10 exceeds 20, so the result is hi. When everything passes, the answer is lo.

questions.q: Print the smallest truck capacity that ships the parcels, in order, within 3 days. Search from the heaviest parcel to the total weight with binary search.
questions.explain: At 67 kg the days are 12 + 30 + 8 (50; adding 25 would exceed), 25 + 17 (42; adding 40 would exceed), and 40 + 5 + 22 (exactly 67): 3 days. At 66 kg the last group no longer fits, so the 22 kg parcel needs a fourth day. The search finds this switch in about 7 checks over the range 40 to 159.

questions.q: Commit c0 is known good and the last commit is known bad. testsFail(i) is expensive. Using binary search over positions 1 to the end, print the first failing commit and how many test runs it took.
questions.explain: ⌈log₂ 299⌉ = 9 at most; this history needs 8 runs, against 211 when stepping forward from the good commit. This is git bisect in miniature.

questions.q: The ring buffer of ping minutes is sorted but rotated. Print the positions of 720, 910 and 715 (or -1), in O(log n), by deciding at each step which half is sorted.
questions.explain: If items[lo] <= items[mid] the left half is sorted and a range check says whether the target can be there; otherwise the right half is sorted. Either way one comparison discards half.

questions.q: Print the position of the oldest (smallest) timestamp in the rotated ring buffer, and in an array that is not rotated, using binary search.
questions.explain: "At most the last element" is false before the rotation point and true from it on. Its first true is the oldest entry; an unrotated array gives 0.

questions.q: A job of p pages at s pages per hour takes Math.ceil(p / s) hours, one job at a time. Print the slowest speed that finishes all jobs within 8 hours, and within 4 hours.
questions.explain: Speeds from 1 to the largest job are the candidates; faster never takes longer, so the check is monotonic. With 4 hours for 4 jobs, each job must take one hour, so the speed must be at least 150.

questions.q: Each unit costs ₦1,850 (185,000 kobo); every order adds a ₦1,500 delivery fee, and 7.5% VAT is added on top (rounded to the kobo). Print the largest quantity whose total fits a ₦50,000 budget, then check it and the next quantity against the budget.
questions.explain: "Too expensive" is false, then true, as the quantity grows. Its first true minus one is the largest affordable quantity. Printing the check on both sides of the answer proves it is the switch point.

questions.q: In the sorted price list, print the first and last position of each price as [first, last], or null if it is absent, using two binary searches (lower and upper bound).
questions.explain: Lower bound is the first position with a price ≥ the target; upper bound is the first with a price > it. The last position is upper − 1, and equal bounds mean the price is absent.
